[[RunningHead]]

Metaphor and Metonymy as the Basis of a New Psychoanalytic Language

Antal Borbely M.D.

Antal Borbely

Antal Borbely  

Metaphors are “in terms of” relationships whereas metonymies are “stands for” or “belongs to” relationships. These relationships are basic on the linguistic, mental, and developmental level. They are therefore suitable for a psychoanalytic framework language capable of uniting the psychoanalytic schools and achieving a rapprochement to those cognitive sciences which already see the mind's functioning as based on metaphor and metonymy. Psychoanalysis with its dialectic between past, present, and future yields a temporal dimension to metaphor: Mentation at one time is understood in terms of mentation at another time—therefore metaphorically (“in terms of”). If metaphoric “in terms of” flexibility is lost, a metonymic (neurotic) “stands for” or “belongs to” relationship holds between issues rooted in different times. It is this temporal dimension of metaphor and metonymy which can conceptually bridge the cognitive sciences with psychoanalysis. The main psychodynamic concepts transference, interpretation, and defense, if slightly reformulated, become relevant within and without the treatment setting. They all can be seen as relating issues from different times flexibly (metaphorically) or neurotically (metonymically) with each other. This leads to conceptualizing transference, interpretation, and defense as having two variants: A metaphoric (healthy) and metonymic (neurotic) one. Psychoanalytic theory was burdened by a one-sided focus on clarification at the expense of enigmatization, both being important aspects of metaphor. The enigmatization, not understood in its theoretical centrality, was therefore collectively enacted as a Babel-like confusion between psychoanalytic languages. The central importance of metaphor and metonymy was not theorized.

Epilogue

S. Montana Katz

S. Montana Katz

S. Montana Katz  

Epilogue

There is agreement on the use of metaphoric processes to conceptualize aspects of experience, as a clinical tool and about the necessity of metaphor in theory formation and structure. Each psychoanalytic perspective employs metaphors specific to the articulation of its theoretical and technical principles. The articles in this issue demonstrate that conceptions of metaphoric processes can address the underlying formulations of unconscious processes used in each perspective. This, then, affords a basis for common ground. An avenue for further exploration and discussion is to seek a link between the use of unconscious metaphoric processes with the use of concepts that capture the nature of clinical process. This would further extend the formulation of a comprehensive structure for the common ground among perspectives. This work will be the subject of a subsequent issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry on metaphoric processes and psychoanalytic fields.

S. Montana Katz

Prologue

Lester Lenoff LCSW

Lester Lenoff

Lester Lenoff  

Prologue

The Prologue to Part 1 of this issue opened with a bowl of spaghetti and sauce. This issue opens closer to the bone, with a band of cannibals. They are enjoying a meal; the entrée is a member of another tribe.

Paulo de Andrade, the Brazilian modernist artist, quoted by Ricardo Bernardi in this issue, proposed that a community responds to the challenge of “outside” products by “cannibalizing” the products of other cultures along with the products of its own past. As Bernardi writes: “Which morsels of Kohut did I cannibalize and which did I let pass?” In the 21st century, psychoanalytic tribes, or communities, differ over era, geography, and core beliefs. Part 2 reflects the extent to which Heinz Kohut's body (body of work, that is) has been served up or left behind.

Paul Ornstein is the editor of The Search for the Self, Kohut's collected papers, which includes his comprehensive discussions (Ornstein, 1978, 1990) of Kohut's evolution from ego psychology to a psychoanalytic psychology of the self. His résumé presents a thriving list of publications, many of which are collaborations with his wife, Anna.

Ornstein begins by reminding the reader of Kohut's initial statement of the centrality of empathy to psychoanalysis: Empathy not only permits a prolonged, sustained “entry” into the inner world of the patient, it also designates the boundaries of psychoanalysis as a “pure psychology.” But Ornstein seeks to go further, addressing, through a clinical illustration, “the question we have raised about the function of empathy in the treatment process.”

Ricardo Bernardi's article describes how, during his control analysis of “Pablo,” the integration of Kohut's concepts of empathy and a mirroring selfobject transference allowed the analysis to move beyond a two-year stalemate into an ultimately successful treatment. The narrative of this clinical passage vibrates with scenes of color, shape, and emotion that reflect the literary ambience of the Río de la Plata, shared by Pablo his analyst, and could stand, on its own strengths, as fiction or a screenplay.

[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Lester Lenoff LCSW

Lester Lenoff

Lester Lenoff  

Epilogue

The meal is over, and Andrade's cannibals, having tasted psychoanalytic fare, are now struck by the compulsion, novel and uncanny, to reflect on their experience. What can they take away from it? Or, cannibals ourselves, what can we take away from it?

I would like, first, to thank my contributors for the nourishment I have taken from editing this issue and invite the reader to the same feast. Finally allowing myself the opportunity to step back from the texts, I am amazed with the breadth and the depth of the knowledge, of the wisdom, I have taken in. A number of the contributors to this issue are my colleagues and friends from a time before I began this project, to whom I have grown closer. And I have gained new colleagues and made new friends as I have gone through the process of putting this issue together.

Each contributor is, to a lesser or greater degree, an outsider to my idiosyncratic take on clinical process. And in my own cannibalistic pursuit of their essence, I believe I have identified a flavor that runs through all the chapters. And I believe that if an analyst or therapist, however much an outsider, approached any of them with an illustration of good clinical work, they would take an interest. And so long as that work led to therapeutic action, they would, like all good cannibals, take off a bite big enough to chew and taste.

The articles here and in Part 1 speak for themselves. Little is to be gained by suggesting that any of the contributors should have thought or responded differently. The sole exception to this is my article devoted to a different way of thinking about Slochower's work with Karen. I hope the reader will visit my framework, as I hope the reader will visit all the frameworks presented. But I am less interested in a wholesale supplanting of other analytic orientations by my own than in wondering how analysts and therapists can and do learn from what their colleagues have written.

I believe that analysts and therapists can learn from their reading in a number ways. The first is through a form, conscious or unconscious, of identification. Does the clinician or patient presented remind me of my own reflections and experience? And given that the parties and process involved in any course of treatment differ, how does that difference, however slight, widen my thinking or practice.

Lester Lenoff

Lester Lenoff

Lester Lenoff  

Part I

It is in the nature of a sauce to obscure some of its ingredients. Beyond the citations to Kohut in this issue, are there implicit themes that have been quietly integrated into the thinking and practice of the contributors. I believe this to be the case.

The analysts contributing to this issue (the contributors) share in having integrated the aspect of Kohut that is procedurally relational. Reis's use of Husserl's phenomenology as a lens to view Kohut establishes this formally. The other contributors make use of this perspective without commenting on it.

Carr and Cortina begin by linking Bowlby with Kohut in the belief that “responsiveness to a child's needs for comfort and protection plays a crucial role in the child's psychological development … of either healthy adjustment or psychopathology” (this issue, p. 42). And the ambience created by the contributors renders the (still vital) presumption that psychopathology derives from innate unconscious fantasies conspicuous by its absence. Malin makes explicit reference to Dr. A's abusive father and Mollon to Elizabeth's “sense of despair at feeling her life is not her own—and I relate this to her recurrent childhood experience” (this issue, p. 37). But the winning case is made by Kitron, eliciting a reader's identification with a traumatized child's need for a responsive parent: the girl who had to tell her story to her mother over and over again; and the boy who needed to have a supportive father or no father at all.

But belief that the roots of psychopathology, in developmental time,1 are in lived experience is not always accompanied the belief that a patient's subjectivity in clinical time derives from lived experience. Stolorow, Atwood, and Orange (2001) note that Fairbairn's theory shares with Kohut's the insistence that psychic structure derives from “early patterns of experienced interaction with others. … [Yet Fairbairn's] endopsychic world, once established, is … a mind whose dynamisms are insulated from the constitutive impact of the surround” (p. 471). Similarly, Sullivan's theory included, along with an intersubjective perspective, the concept of parataxic distortion [emphasis original], a process through which a person's current experiences of others are said to be “warped” [emphasis added] in consequence of his or her past interpersonal history … 1Susan Fox Horn (personal communication, 2005) suggested the term developmental time to complement clinical time.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

S. Montana Katz

S. Montana Katz

S. Montana Katz  

Prologue

This issue is intended to comprise and generate further dialogue about psychoanalytic theory and practice in this polyperspectival era that is inclusive of multiple analytic perspectives and allows for interdisciplinary interaction. Because in the current situation there still is no generally accepted common conceptual or technical ground between psychoanalytic perspectives, the concept of unconscious metaphoric processes was selected for this issue to explore whether it can serve the purpose. Every analytic perspective that agrees with the existence and influence of some form of unconscious processes is likely to be able to assent to a psychoanalytic conception of unconscious metaphoric process. With the use of this concept as basic, it was hoped, that conference and dialogue between the different analytic perspectives about psychoanalytic theory and practice will be possible without loss or confusion of meaning. It was further hoped that, ultimately, the result would be an expanded potential for the integration of concepts, principles, and techniques across analytic positions.

Such a project is of contemporary relevance and perhaps urgency. In the current climate of diminished status, recognition of, and educational outlets for, psychoanalytic thought and practice, together with other current global and clinical factors along with the lack of communication among the multiple branches of analytic theory and practice, it is unclear if there remains an integrated field of psychoanalysis. This situation is unacceptable if psychoanalysis, as a body of theory and as a clinical set of techniques for addressing issues in mental health, is to thrive. Over the past decades, there have been repeated calls to find a common ground and to open genuine discourse and understanding between the analytic perspectives.

Finding common ground among the different, and at some points mutually inconsistent, psychoanalytic perspectives could potentially lead to powerful theoretical and clinical tools. The articulation of shared concepts, principles, or assumptions may lead to the development of a purely psychoanalytic framework and language. At the basis of such a language would be concepts and terms with which the fundamental principles of each perspective could be expressed without loss of meaning. Moreover, then, dialogue among the different perspectives would be possible in such a way that the meanings of the terms used would be as transparent as possible. An umbrella for psychoanalysis could be found in this framework, in which disagreements may not dissolve but will be clearer and more fully understood. Both similarities and differences among the different psychoanalytic perspectives may be clarified with such a model.

Reading Kohut Through Husserl

Bruce Reis Ph.D.

Bruce Reis


Bruce Reis   Bruce Reis, Ph.D., is a member of the North American Editorial Board of The International Journal of Psychoanalysis and a member of the faculty of the NYU Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis.

Introduction

“As primal ego, I constitute my horizon of transcendental others as cosubjects within the transcendental intersubjectivity which constitutes the world” [Husserl, 1970, p. 184].

Kohut's introduction of the empathic method has been both lauded and critiqued. At once recognized as a significant advance in psychoanalytic clinical technique, the empathic method has also come under fire for ultimately remaining within a one-person model of psychic functioning. In this article, I wish to reexamine Kohut's introduction of the method of empathy as vicarious introspection by taking up the seminal 1959 paper in which that term was introduced, and briefly augmenting that paper with some of Kohut's later writing on empathy. My purpose will not be to enter the ongoing debate as to whether empathy, itself, is curative or whether it reengages stalled developmental processes. I will instead concentrate on Kohut's initial presentation of empathy as a method of inquiry, in order to reassess whether claims that his was a one-person psychology hold true; and to better understand what it was that might have been meant by Kohut in his consideration of the objective and scientific use of empathy in the clinical situation. Empathy as an epistemological avenue leading to knowledge of the other, is what I wish to further investigate. Admittedly, I seek to create a retrospective reading of Kohut that may not follow his work chapter and verse, but may find in that work the seeds of what will later flower as postclassical relational theory.

It is clear that Kohut strongly advocated the employment of empathy as a facet of what he termed a scientific endeavor. As a mode of observation, Kohut (1959) did not neglect the fact that this “observational method defines the contents and the limits of the observed field” and later would more firmly locate the analyst within this field (Kohut, 1984, p. 465). Kohut (1979) claimed that it was through this empathic methodology that he was able to “perceive meanings, or the significance of meanings, I had formerly not consciously perceived” (p. 3). But his early use of language concerning fact finding, and truth claims made through the method of vicarious introspection have garnered strong critique for what reads as his definitive grasp of knowledge of others. Epilogue: Psychoanalysis From the Inside—Our Own Analyses

Carol Levin

Carol Levin

Carol Levin  

Epilogue: Psychoanalysis From the Inside—Our Own Analyses

Psychoanalysis has been good to me and I can be as respectful of personal limitations as I can be optimistic about each mind's latent potential to continue its own unique development [after formal analysis ends]… . My present life feels enriched and more satisfying … . all now seems speakable … .

—Austin Silber (1996)

The articles in this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry speak to the experiences of four different analysts for whom analysis nurtured rich processes of growth and development. These writers didn't find their analyses to be smooth sailing, nor would some of their analyses be seen as following the “book” (Hoffman, 1994, p. 188). But each was as committed to psychoanalysis as their analysts were, and each found their way of weathering the storms that emerged in their lives and their analyses, sometimes cocreated by each analytic pair, to arrive at their own unique transformations.

After the sudden death of her first analyst, Deutsch found her way to a second analysis in which she did much more than metabolize and mourn the loss of her beloved first analyst. Wixom used her analyst's unconventional gift as an affirmation, inspiration, and organizer of her growth. Bornstein used disciplined self-analysis after he internalized the analytic method to articulate his own theory of analytic process. And in a process of soft assembly, Levin found and created experiences within as well as outside the analytic dyad that promoted her growth as a person and an analyst.

Growth, as these four papers reflect, is the goal of a good-enough analysis and can be viewed through the lens of complex systems theory as a unique, nonlinear, dynamic process1 that unfolds within and sometimes beyond the constrains of what is possible for each analytic pair over time (Coburn, this issue). Analysis thus has been good enough to these four analyst-writers, who each, as Elise writes in this issue, took the “huge risk [of] enter[ing] psychoanalytic treatment,” as we all have. They opened themselves to a “relationship, an ever-present dialogue, with [their] analyst [in a] unique partnership [that] has the potential to engage … hearts and minds … more … than any relationship since early childhood.” Then these writers assumed the additional risk of daring to write about the intimacies and imperfections of their unique analytic journeys. They made their 1A dynamic systems perspective has important implications for our understanding of development. As Galatzer-Levy (2002) writes, “complex systems and their associated non-linear dynamics predict a … world with abrupt changes, discontinuities, idiosyncratic developmental lines, and disproportions between causes and effects [that] suggest new possibilities for the psychoanalytic model of change and development” (p. 419). These “include discontinuous, sudden and qualitative shifts not only in manifest behavior but also in in-depth psychological functioning” (p. 419). Galatzer-Levy (2002) argues from within such a complex systems model that it is not the details of development but the fact of development that is important and that development is the marker of a good-enough analysis.

Soft Assembly: Expanding the Field of Therapeutic Actions in (My Training) Analysis

Carol Levin

Carol Levin

Carol Levin  

The author's project in this article is to wrestle with a paradox—how it happened that she changed while in a training analysis that moved into and, after a fashion, remained in lockdown. Things began to make sense when she happened upon complexity theory. Simultaneously an analysand, a becoming-analyst with her first patient, and a supervisee, she expands the field of therapeutic actions in (her) analysis and illuminates from the inside how therapeutic change is an emergent property of intertwining, interpenetrating, and interacting dynamic systems. She has come to see her growth within this expanded field as a fluid, contingent, and novel process of soft assembly.

Discussion

Ana-María Rizzuto M.D.

Ana-María Rizzuto

Ana-María Rizzuto  

The aim of my discussion is to assess whether the author's contributions are apt to support the notion that the metaphoric process offers a common ground for dialogue among psychoanalytic schools. I have been asked to focus on theoretical considerations.

Common ground means that at least a majority of psychoanalytic perspectives consider the metaphoric process essential for the understanding of the psychoanalytic process and for the theoretical understanding of the mind. Difficult questions face me as a discussant of theoretical issues: Where does metaphor fit in psychoanalytic theory? Waelder (1962) stated that psychoanalytic theory is composed of “different parts which have different degrees of relevance” (p. 619). Metaphor appears first at the level of observation manifesting many aspects of the configuration of the patient's mind. The level of clinical interpretation introduces the first obvious complexity for the understanding of each particular metaphor or metaphoric activity. The interpenetration of words, feelings, and actions during an analytic moment requires that metaphor or the metaphoric process be understood, synchronically and diachronically, as opening up the meaning they might have as a psychic event for both participants. The collective effort of the analytic community has always tried to organize into a comprehensive understanding the repeated appearance of similar phenomena into generalizations at the clinical level, classifying them—usually under a metaphoric term—as group of phenomena that form particular configurations be it of symptoms, type of experience or other groupings. The next theoretical stage allows the formulation of clinical theories and concepts that have explanatory value for the understanding of the other three levels. Concepts emerge that have ubiquitous usefulness as dynamic metaphors such as repression, regression or defense. Finally, Freud's positivistic philosophy offers a way of dealing with the world by using the power of reason to better the human condition.

[[RunningHead]]

PROLOGUE

Lester Lenoff

Lester Lenoff

Lester Lenoff  

Part I

There is a science fiction time-travel story that I read as a boy, long before I started noting down titles and authors for future citation. The main character is introduced to time travel and uses it extensively. When he attempts to return permanently to the time and place where he began, he is involuntarily swept back into the cosmic warp that has become his temporal passageway. There, his initial guide explains to him that time is like a bowl of spaghetti with its strands wrapped around each other. If you accomplish too many jumps between strands, you become part of the sauce.

Has Heinz Kohut become part of the sauce?

Outside the self psychological community, Heinz Kohut's name has not maintained a profile in the 1990s and 2000s. Yet some writers, pre-eminently Judith Teicholtz (2006), maintain that Kohut has been “quietly” integrated into mainstream practice, as well as having served a catalyst in the development of postmodern schools of psychoanalysis (p. 49).

Australians Donald Grant and Edwin Harari assert that not only the clinical practice of empathy, but theoretical constructs that add up to empathy, without naming it, predated Kohut's privileging it in a psychoanalytic psychology of the self. Freud (1921) encapsulated the concept, defining empathy as “the mechanism by means of which we are enabled to take up any attitude at all towards another mental life” (p. 110) but consigned this, his single reference to empathy, to a footnote. Grant and Harari trace empathy-by-another-name through the theory of the English School, relate the concept of empathy to the recent discovery of mirror neurons, and provide a clinical illustration of the way empathy enters clinical practice.

David Kitron, from Tel Aviv, provides narrative, clinical, and scriptural perspectives on the centrality of empathy to life. Kitron concentrates on the responsibility—analyst to patient, parent to child, and person to person—to respond with empathy. Kitron allows for the possibility that empathy will be unwelcome to the provider or the recipient. Despite this, if the provider is an analyst, the responsibility remains to make use of empathy to discover when the patient requires privacy and to recognize the sometime burden of offering empathy while maintaining the clinical priority of the patient's well-being.

On Childlessness

Nancy Kulish Ph.D.

Nancy Kulish

Nancy Kulish  

This article explores the experience of childlessness in individuals who want children. Psychoanalytic literature has documented many psychic meanings of childlessness. The author focuses on one factor that has not received much attention: a loss of connection to early objects and continuity with one's past and future. The author provides several clinical cases—both male and female, as well as a discussion of the life and work of the famous artist, Frida Kahlo, to demonstrate how childlessness can rob the individual of a way of coping with his or her fears about death. The author speculates on the sense of the inevitability of death as a driving force toward procreation.

Based on a John Sayles 2003 movie, Casa de Los Babys, about adoption in South America, the author uses the characters portrayed and references to the haunting music lyrics, to focus on the grief over the specter of the end of these 6 women's psychological and biological attempts to conceive their own offspring. responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein M.D.

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Epilogue

Creating connections between past, present, future, and the self by procreating is how humans grapple with death and the limitations of life. This theme, described by Kulish, reverberates in all the other articles, reflecting the inexorable power of a life force, which Freud (1920) described in Beyond the Pleasure Principle. He described this life force as part of a duality with a death force where death always wins out.

From a philosophical perspective, he may have been correct, but from the perspective of living human beings, life always wins as long as we are alive and, since we cannot comprehend death while we are alive, all we have is life and our creativity in dealing with death. This issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry is a loud statement of the pervasiveness of life over death in human nature. Freud wrote pessimistically about the overbearing power of death that has reverberated in the analytic literature ever since, especially in clinical psychoanalysis, although 100 years since writing, we are still vitally thinking and debating over his creative endeavor about the place of the death force in life.

Melvin Bornstein, M.D.

Issue Editor

Discussion of Jean Wixom's “Just Do It”

Philip Ringstrom

Philip Ringstrom

Philip Ringstrom  

Jean Wixom's article “Just Do It” is a poignant story, frequently painfully so. It is a tale that helps one understand how wonderful a deeply committed psychoanalysis can be in transforming one's life. By that, I actually mean the lives of both analysand and analyst, not to mention affecting all the other people in their lives. This is a story about Jean and her analyst's commitment to not allowing her to flee treatment for the host of reasons—both real and psychological—that would send most individuals scrambling for the exit. If resistance ever needed any ammunition, Jean had an unimpeachable excuse for avoiding the painful work facing her. Here's a capsulation of her story and then some thoughts of what we might make of it.

Her opening sentence tells all: “It was a month after beginning my analysis when my husband's cancer was discovered in its advanced stage.” Her tale begins like the crack of a 2×4 hitting us square in the forehead. This “virginal” analysis, she notes, began as an “exhilarating experience.” It clearly differed from all her previous, though helpful, psychotherapies. This time, however, it differed not only because she was finally ready for it, she had also found the right analyst with whom to have it. He exhibited the right blend of “balance and directness and reserve” along with “his pithy, spot-on remarks,” a blend that captivated her curiosity from the start. It doesn't get much better than this, which brackets all the more painfully the calamitous news of her husband's life-threatening diagnosis. One might call this one of life's “cheap tricks,” that is, to present one with the very circumstance that they had all their lives hungered for (both wittingly and not), only to then say, “Sorry, not for you!” Thankfully, much to Jean's analyst's credit and her willingness to be helped, they both stared back at cruel fate and said, “I don't think so!”

It was not at all as easy as my glib commentary suggests. It was excruciating for Jean to have to be “a virtual single parent, wage earner, nurse, and medical advocate.” That's plenty enough for both Jean and her analyst to say, “Probably not a great time for an analysis; maybe we should wait until the ‘dust settles.’” But this would have been a lie and both knew it, though her analyst had to press Jean to see it. Creative Self-Revitalization: Discussion of Mel Bornstein's “A Psychoanalyst's Story: A Simple Discovery After Years of Searching”

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Throughout the health care reform debate that occurred in the United States in 2009, President Obama reiterated: If you are satisfied with the health insurance program you have, you can keep it. If not, it is desirable to have an alternative. Mel Bornstein was not satisfied with the analyses he had, so he found an alternative in his regular organized program of self-analysis. Nor was Mel satisfied with the theory that guided his analysis, so he found an alternative in pluralism—essentially creating his own experience-near theory amalgam.

Mel begins his article by telling the reader what he has discovered. For his patients, himself, and many of us, the goal is to embrace all of life. The process is to take possession of injurious traumas and reveal them in an intimate relationship. Note the active verbs: embrace, take possession, and reveal. The key is at the end: an intimate relationship. While the key is stated at the end, maybe the key, the intimate relationship, is also the beginning, middle, and the neverending.

An intimate relationship requires the capacity and willingness of two people to participate. The arid quality of Mel's second analysis guided by neutrality, abstinence, and anonymity, is painful to read, and to remember. We analysts can only read Mel's article through our own experience, and where the pain is shared, the story achieves an intimacy between teller and reader. Intimacy comes easily to some analytic pairs and is more difficult for others to achieve. Humiliation and shame—powerful affects that in the past have often largely ignored as centrally motivating emotions—exist on both sides of the couch. Consequently, analyst and analysand can each hide from themselves and each other—analysts behind a theory of technique, patients behind a wall they often don't even know they have created.

An artifact for me as reader and discussant of Mel's paper is that I have an intimate relationship with Mel. As friends and partners, we have created and worked together on Psychoanalytic Inquiry for 30-plus years. I tease him about his indestructible (and sometimes I believe misplaced) optimism. And so to read about his being anxious, withdrawn, and devitalized moves him from “my Mel” to “patient Mel.

The Nonverbal Unconscious: Collision and Collusion of Metaphor

Robert White M. D.

Robert White

Robert White  

Adopting the Lakoff and Johnson view that conceptual systems of the mind are inherently metaphoric and embodied, I examine theoretical metaphor in psychoanalytic theory as an example of the use of metaphor more generally in the mind. I have chosen concepts of the nondynamic unconscious to explore representative metaphors. These include the theories of W. Bion, C. and S. Botella, and D. Stern. This article first outlines recent interest in the nondynamic unconscious and then examines the theories of Bion, the Botellas, and Stern in detail. Differences and similarities among the theoretical metaphors are explored. I suggest that theoretical metaphors progress both through the attempted destruction of existing metaphor and reshaping of existing metaphor into new meanings. I am interested in finding among the metaphoric collisions that there may be hidden collusions that can potentially lead to unifying concepts.

Procreation—A Discussion

Joseph Lichtenberg M.D.

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Procreation—babies. Having babies, not having babies (Kulish). Deciding to not have a baby (Stuart). Not being able to have a baby, then being able to have a baby through fertilization (Abassi, Notman). Adopting a baby (Balsam). Not being able to adopt a baby (Balsam). Being pregnant (Otte). Giving birth to a creation, rather than procreation (Stuart). And for each, a plethora of conscious and unconscious meanings. And for each, a challenge to the continuity and productivity of an analysis.

In the paradoxical fashion in which pathology seems to draw much of our analytic attention, more of the content of this issue on procreation is about failures in having babies, rather than successes. Kulish's excellent lead paper focuses on childlessness. Beginning with Lear's curse on his daughter Goneril: “Into her womb convey sterility!” Kulish describes the depressive, mournful, tragic state of three women in their forties, Frida Kahlo's unforgettable artistic rendering of the agony of miscarriage, and a man who decried his failure to extend his lineage. Kulish and the authors that follow select the treatment of procreation they choose to develop to edify an analytic readership, but I note the absence of references to the quiet joy or exuberant fulfillment of many pregnancies and births. As an example of the positive affective turn on by the experience of pregnancy and birth (in this case twins), I can cite my patient Sonya, whose previous severe depression and avoidance of men I have described (Lichtenberg, 2005; Lichtenberg, Lachmann, and Fosshage, 2002). Sonya's becoming pregnant also exemplifies a positive utilization of artificial reproductive treatment (ART) about which Notman has written a remarkable “textbook” primer I would advise every colleague to use to educate themselves and their patients. My experience with Sonya introduces another factor for outcome that may have been lacking in a number of the problematic cases (Abbasi, Kulish, Otte, Stuart) and stories (Balsam)—the presence of a strong support system: her husband, sensitive women friends, and her continuing, now mostly supportive, treatment.

Metaphor as Conflict, Conflict as Metaphor

Léon Wurmser Ph.D.h.c.

Léon Wurmser

Léon Wurmser  

This article deals with a double idea: Metaphor itself, by bridging two domains of experience, lives in the tension, even contradictoriness, of what it brings together, and in that way may be uniquely suited to present a theory of mental life that centers on inner polarities and antitheses, i.e., inner conflict in a wide sense, not necessarily bound to the drive or structural metaphors. In turn, the concept of conflict itself entails a spectrum of warlike or violent metaphors, such as defense, antitheses, clashing values or forces, being torn or broken apart, inner part personalities fighting with each other, etc. The history of the metaphors for various forms of inner conflict are traced back in Western and Eastern literature (Homer, Plato, the Bible, the Talmud, St. Augustine, Confucius, and Lao Tzu), thus broadening the search for a common ground for psychoanalytic perspectives.

Jennifer Stuart Ph.D.

Jennifer Stuart

Jennifer Stuart  

This article explores the interplay of one woman's decision not to have children with the development of her successful creative career. In her story, we hear how a desire for children may both inspire and impede creative accomplishment. Though creative work may serve, in part, to express procreative wishes, the products of that work are not mere substitutes for babies. Creativity in other domains offers gratifications distinct from—and not lesser than—the pleasures of motherhood. As analysts, we would do well to remember that for many women, adult development can proceed satisfactorily along pathways that do not include motherhood.

This article explores and discusses Carol Levin's psychoanalytic journey, her personal struggles and transformations, and her conceptualizations of them through the lens of psychoanalytic complexity theory. It examines the nature of complex relational systems with attention paid to the concepts of system constraint and system freedom. It argues that personal transformation and growth are products and properties of larger, interpenetrating, complex systems in which each of us is relentlessly embedded and that loss and grief are inevitably essential components of personal development in the context of human relational systems. Holding, Collaborating, Colliding: A Cross Theoretical Conversation

Joyce Slochower Ph.D.

Joyce Slochower

Joyce Slochower  

Lester Lenoff's thoughtful article explores the intersection of my work on holding with some core Kohutian ideas. Lenoff offers a respectful consideration of our perspectives—their overlaps—and their divergences. It's important to preface my response, I think, with a clear acknowledgment of the pitfalls of cross-theoretical conversations. Kohutian theory has its own jargon, quite different from mine. Less immersed in its nuances, I approach it from the outside in and, in so doing, there's the danger of misapprehension, of smoothing out and exaggerating differences, that is, of confusion of tongues. I think of holding my way; you view the selfobject function in yours and as we try to bridge our perspectives, something gets lost in translation. With this caveat, I plunge in, hopeful that dialogue will allow us to refine and delineate areas of overlap and difference.

In his discussion, Lenoff refers to Relational theory. Relational theory, like self psychology, has expanded in multiple directions over the years; it is an umbrella term that has many facets and resists reification. For this reason, I prefer to use a small r in discussing it. And because both self psychology and relational theory are really theories rather than unitary positions, I limit myself here to Lenoff's exploration of my writing about holding as it interfaces with his Kohutian perspective. I do not address the broader question of differences between Kohutian thinking and other aspects of relational theory, nor do I consider my overlap with contemporary self psychological models. I begin with a detour into the relational critique of holding and then turn to the relationship between Lenoff's Kohutian theory and my own work.

THE HOLDING METAPHOR IN A RELATIONAL CONTEXT

By the mid-1950s, Winnicott (e.g., 1955) and other members of the British Middle Group were using the holding metaphor to describe the parallel between maternal care and the analyst-patient relationship. The Winnicottian mother/analyst protected the very vulnerable baby/patient from noxious environmental impingements in an effort to contact early failures and support access to previously hidden true self experience.1That idea generated a powerful response. If the analyst 1Although Winnicott is most frequently associated with work on the holding process, many others have also contributed to the concept of holding or containment, including Bion (1959; 1962, 1963), Little (1960), Loewald (1960), Sandler (1960), Khan (1963), Balint (1968), Kohut, (1971), Bollas (1978), and Sandback (1993).

The Tao of Self Psychology: Was Heinz Kohut a Taoist Sage?

Farrell Silverberg N.C.Psy.A.

Farrell Silverberg

Farrell Silverberg  

Because humanity is present in the heart, it becomes active as soon as it is affected, just as seeds sprout as soon as they are affected. (Chang Po-Hsing, cited in Hsi, 1175, p. 8)1

When Heinz Kohut died, I was just becoming familiar with his writings and did not yet realize how significantly his mission to integrate introspecting empathy into psychoanalytic work would figure in my own eventhal search to do the same. It was not until my return from training with a Buddhist-Taoist psychotherapy teacher in Korea, many years later, that I truly began to deeply appreciate that, in his search for the infusion of empathy, humility, and humanity into our psychoanalytic treatment of patients, Kohut had led the way for all those in our field seeking to similarly imbue our work with these noble truths.

These highest of human capacities, when intentionally cultivated and integrated in psychoanalysis, are as much rooted in the wisdom of the East as the psychological science of the West. Sometimes such simple truths get lost in translation, or in our various ways of operating in self psychological, relational, and other analytic language, concepts, and techniques. Therefore, in this article, I endeavor to bring empathic ideas more fully to the forefront and examine whether, in conducting his inner and interpersonal exploration of the psychotherapy environment, Kohut functioned as a psychoanalytic Taoist sage for our profession who pointed the way to the future of integrating heart and mind in ourselves as practitioners and consequently in our patients.

In 1957, Kohut presented a paper at the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis on the topics of introspection and empathy. In this paper, he pointed out that there might exist in analysts a general resistance against introspection, and especially against an empathic introspection that was reminiscent of Eastern inner reflective and meditative traditions. Procedural Interpretation: A Method of Working Between the Lines in the Nonverbal Realm

Bruce Herzog M.D.

Bruce Herzog

Bruce Herzog  

INTRODUCTION

Throughout the last century, verbal interpretation has been an inseparable companion to the process of psychoanalysis, and the ability to interpret effectively continues to be highly valued by psychoanalysts. Today many of us can convincingly argue that a thoughtful, well-timed interpretation still constitutes the most significant therapeutic event that can occur in an analysis.

Our acknowledgment of the importance of spoken interpretation can have its disadvantages, though. Efforts to fine-tune our ability to convey understanding by verbal means may run the risk of disavowing another essential aspect of our clinical work: namely that of nonverbal activities, which themselves can have a very powerful therapeutic impact. That we sometimes have difficulty finding the language to describe these activities and may occasionally neglect them shouldn't surprise us—nonverbal issues seem to be the stuff of intuition, not objective discourse. In most relationships, much of what is going on nonverbally is usually not talked about directly—it is simply experienced between the lines. Regardless of any tendency to overlook them, these between-the-lines, nonverbal events can contribute significantly both in achieving understanding, and communicating that understanding to our patients. In fact, I believe that a therapist needs to demonstrate his thinking through his behavior as a necessary adjunct to communicating with words. In this way, I hope to elevate the realm of behavior to be equal to the realm of language in the interpretive process.

TWO DIMENSIONS OF PSYCHOANALYTIC ACTIVITY: PROCEDURAL AND SYMBOLIC

Our discussion calls for the observation of two dimensions of experience within the psychoanalytic setting: one mediated by words and the other by action. Finding the Pot of Gold: Using Psychotherapy to Assist the Emotional Development of a Four-Year-Old Girl Diagnosed With Asperger's Disorder

J. Shaft

J. Shaft

J. Shaft  

This article illustrates the development of a working alliance between a psychoanalytic psychotherapist and a four-year-old girl, Elsa, diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome. From the beginning, intense anxiety related and reactive to Asperger's was central to the treatment process. My nonimpinging presence and curiosity, and use of transference–countertransference phenomena were central in the development and deepening of the therapeutic relationship. In the encouragement and safety of the three-times-weekly therapy schedule, Elsa began to play out her fantasies, which led to a process of active developmental growth. Over the course of the first three years of treatment, Elsa became more openly involved in the therapeutic relationship. Her anxiety diminished as she began to tolerate her own affective experience. She began to experience greater success and comfort in social interactions with her family and other people in her life.

[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Katharine Gould L.C.S.W.

Katharine Gould

Katharine Gould  

Epilogue

Neurobiological advances have clarified that it's nature, not nurture, that causes Asperger's syndrome (AS) or autistic spectrum disorders. The case reports of these authors and my own clinical work show how effective a psychoanalytically informed perspective can be when treating these patients. This perspective works because it recreates the early process of affective attunement between infant and mother, an experience of reciprocity that instills in the child the motivation for attachment and relatedness.

These clinical summaries demonstrate a variety of ways that this attunement process can be recreated in treatment to accommodate the atypical brain of the AS patient—a brain that, because it has great difficulty interpreting the intention of another, cannot experience being seen or found. Lacking this developmental step—of knowing oneself as another knows you—the AS patients described in the preceding pages did not know their own minds, which left them feeling isolated, alien, and unfound.

Recently, in December 2009, I was struck by a New York Times article that reported the following: “Runaway 13-year-old spent 11 days in the subways despite frantic hunt.” This headline described the escape chosen by a boy diagnosed with AS after he was reprimanded in school for not completing an assignment. Finally found after an exhaustive 11-day search (involving police, parents, family friends, and identifying flyers), the boy was asked to comment on his experience and said, “Nobody really cares about the world and about people”—a statement painfully at odds with his mother's response. “I tell him ‘Talk to me. Tell me what you need. If I ever make a mistake, tell me …’ I don't know as a mother how to get to his heart … to find out what hurts.”

This adolescent boy, in the language of our authors, “put his mind into action” and hid among the commuter crowds of the Manhattan subways, where he remained lost for a remarkable expanse of time, successfully proving his point! In a similar way, the patients described here, like the boy on the subway, had remained unseen because they lacked the capacity for spontaneous relatedness. Understanding this, these authors began treatment by teaching reciprocity using methods best suited to the interests and developmental age of their patient. Although the conduit used to access their patient's world varied from the interpretation of a toddler's play to fantasy play, board games, building projects, play-date sessions, insect observation, and, in the case of adults, the modeling of self-revelation to teach self-awareness—the dyadic experience taught these AS patients at all stages of emotional development to understand their own minds and to use them effectively. Once they learned that their actions had meaning and saw themselves in the minds of their therapists, they developed a sense of agency and a beginning capacity to participate in reciprocal relationships.

Asperger's Disorder: Implications for Psychoanalysis

Fred Volkmar

Fred Volkmar

Fred Volkmar  

Although described only one year after Kanner's (1943) classic description of autism, Asperger's account of the condition that now carries his name (Asperger, 1944) has, until recently, received much less attention. Psychoanalytic attention has focused largely on infantile autism. and early work was concerned with the idea that experiential factors might be involved in pathogenesis. During the 1970s, a large body of work questioned this view noting, for example, the strong genetic and brain basis of autism (Volkmar, 2000). Work from other fields began to question some early theoretical notions, e.g., the normative existence of an autistic phase, but important questions that autism raised for understanding early ego development and capacities for self-object differentiation continue to be a concern of some theoretical and clinical interest (Volkmar, 2000). This article provides a summary of Asperger's as a diagnostic concept in terms of the history of the concept, aspects of clinical expression and co-morbidity as well as implications or intervention. The final section of the article focuses on implications that the condition may have for theory and practice.

Talia Weiner

Talia Weiner  

This article shows that psychodynamic perspectives are particularly relevant in working with people who have Asperger's syndrome (AS). It is believed that a central problem among people with AS is difficulty in understanding their own mind and the mind of others. Recent discussion of factors involved in fostering change in psychoanalytic psychotherapy stresses the importance of a theory of mind, known as mentalization, that refers to the effort by the therapist to understand the patient's mind. It is in this demonstration of the activity of coming to know the mind of another that psychodynamic perspectives may be particularly helpful in working with persons with AS to come to understand their own mind and to know the minds of others. Psychodynamic psychotherapy is also important in helping persons with AS to deal with difficulties and frustrations that they have encountered in their life.

[[RunningHead]]

Kohut and Lacan: Mirror Opposites

Barnet Malin M.D.

Barnet Malin

California

Barnet Malin   Barnet D. Malin, M.D., is a training and supervising analyst at the Psychoanalytic Center of California and the New Center for Psychoanalysis in Los Angeles, California. He is an Assistant Clinical Professor in the UCLA/David Geffen School of Medicine.

Introduction

Heinz Kohut and Jacques Lacan shared roles as psychoanalytic theorists who built vital epistemological challenges to the psychoanalytic mainstream into their metapsychological and developmental theories. Their radical emendations were born from their respective dissatisfaction with the theory and practice of American ego psychology. Perhaps most fundamentally, each found that, as practiced at the time, ego psychology foisted the analyst's views of reality on the patient, producing results antithetical to the aim of psychoanalysis. Kohut (1984) wrote: “We believe that the [theories] of drive primacy and drive taming … and [the movement] from narcissism to object love are—or have gradually become—part of a supraordinated moral system in scientific disguise; we therefore believe, verbal disclaimers to the contrary, that the actual practice of analysis is burdened by an admixture of hidden moral and educational goals” (p. 208). Lacan (1954b), critiquing a case vignette given by Ernst Kris, held that Kris's “analysis of the resistances … consists [of] attacking the subject's world (that is, his patterns) in order to reshape it on the model of the analyst's world, in the name of the analysis of defense” (p. 332).

Kohut and Lacan thus came to listen and respond to their patients in new ways, even as each maintained that their aim was to stay within and offer correctives to the psychoanalytic mainstream. Their analytic listening produced several points of overlap. For example, each highlighted the vital “clinical importance of recognition” (Muller, 1989, p. 363); each held that aggression was a secondary or reactive phenomena (Lacan, 1948, Kohut, 1972); and each employed the metaphor of mirroring as a central metapsychological and developmental concept. They listened differently, however, and their respective views of mirroring and a mirror stage stand in stark opposition, marking their point of theoretical divergence and leading towards their opposing views regarding the fundamental nature of the self.

Prologue: Psychoanalysis From the Inside—Our Own Analyses

Carol Levin

Carol Levin

Carol Levin  

Prologue: Psychoanalysis From the Inside—Our Own Analyses

The idea for this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry emerged from conversations with colleagues about our own analyses. It came into my mind that we are in a unique position to explore a treasure trove of first-person data and theorize psychoanalytic process and therapeutic actions from the inside—from inside our (often multiple) analyses and from inside our field. It was a small step to interest the creative and receptive editors of this journal in my idea of asking analysts to illuminate the complex and unique ways that growth happened in their own analyses and how the developmental process begun in analysis continued in time, often moving along in unforeseen, meandering, and creative ways. The process of creating this issue began.

It soon emerged that there was a long distance to travel between talking about our analyses to actually writing about them—no surprise here. Indeed many forces converge to reinforce our reality concerns and our resistances and discourage us from revealing what goes awry in our less-than-successful analyses, or what has been transformative in our successful ones, or what the (usual) balance between the two may have been, all unifying themes of the articles in this issue.

If we are to write in the first person about our analyses, we immediately encounter our narcissistic vulnerability with its accompanying shame and guilt. It is always a risk to expose our frailties and those of our analysts. But frailties are part of our own and our analysts' humanity. Then there are other risks. For some, writing about their analyses may provoke political consequences that could derail desired advancement in analytic institutes. And disclosing our own analytic experiences may have genuine impact on our analysts, on our present and future patients, and always on ourselves as we re-engage with what are often painful feelings.

Just as we thoughtfully and carefully consider the potential impact of personal disclosure on our patients in our clinical work, so must thoughtfulness and care be ever present in how we choose to disclose our personal analytic stories in our writing. But our hubris, expressed in the old myth of being completely analyzed, is hopefully fading away as our collective writings demystify analysis and what exactly is “analytic” (Levin, 2006). With more of us writing about psychoanalysis from the inside, we are deepening our understanding of the complex realities of all analyses and of ourselves as vulnerable patients.

Prologue

Katharine Gould L.C.S.W

Katharine Gould

Katharine Gould  

Notice — The original version of the Prologue by Katharine Gould has been removed, and a corrected version posted here.

“There is from the start an extreme autistic aloneness that whenever possible disregards, ignores, shuts out anything that comes to the child from outside.” (Kanner, 1943)

“I'm stuck in a dark cave, but in my hand I have a laser to cut my way outside” (from the dream of an 11-year-old boy with a diagnosis of Asperger's syndrome, 2010)

The purpose of the contributing authors in this issue is to demonstrate the various effective uses of psychoanalytically informed treatment with patients diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome. Collectively, they demonstrate some of the more inspired and nontraditional methods available. This is a timely issue because, in spite of the considerable progress in diagnosing and treating autistic spectrum disorders, there remains a pervasive and misinformed consensus that psychoanalytic therapy is largely ineffective with these patients.

The two opening quotes, which were expressed almost 70 years apart, encompass the largely unchanged understanding of autism and, most important, as will be illustrated by the articles in this issue, they indicate the recent psychoanalytically informed methods of treatment that have made it possible for some of these patients to experience being found and then to reverse the process by finding us. For the eleven year old dreamer quoted above, the outside world was hardly ignored or disregarded. The laser he used to cut himself free was a metaphor for the empathic understanding and desire for reciprocity that he had experienced and internalized in therapy.

CLINICAL THEORY: IS ASPERGER'S SYNDROME A VARIANT OF AUTISM?

Pertinent to the issue's topic is the recent recommendation by the American Psychiatric Association that Asperger's syndrome should no longer be a separate diagnosis, but instead be included under Autistic Syndrome Disorders in its new authoritative Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-V) to be published in 2013.

Ricardo Bernardi  

INTRODUCTION

Heinz Kohut is not among the authors integrated into the psychoanalytic tradition of the Río de la Plata (Buenos Aires and Montevideo), in which I was trained. Yet his ideas had a considerable influence on my development as a psychoanalyst. I wish to relate, through a clinical example, my initial encounter with Kohut's work and the challenge raised, in a key moment of my training, by an author whose concepts differed from those of my analytic community.

Analysts inevitably respond to a variety of influences and struggle to integrate them in a coherent way. But the conceptual compatibility of differing theories is a complex problem and its different dimensions are not always sufficiently examined. Addressing this issue, this article aims both to describe a case from my training (1975–1980) that was particularly evocative of Kohut's ideas, but also to look back from the present (2010), at the way in which I tried to combine Kohut with theories that were already a part of my training.

It is not easy to translate the conceptual language from one psychoanalytic school to that of another. This difficulty, along with the inertia of local tradition, likely accounts for the infrequency of systematic revisions of analytic thinking about a particular issue. The range of ideas presented in psychoanalytic texts is typically limited to concepts already familiar to the author. This limits the sources of innovation to the ideas of an author and others who already agree on theory, and increases the isolation of the various schools. Psychoanalytic training reinforces and extends this situation because most institutes reinforce a local tradition, ignoring innovations deriving from outside. But, at times, the ideas of one creative author break through the barriers and are received by analysts from other communities. I believe that the challenges derived from this phenomenon deserve to be studied.

Asperger's Syndrome: A Mixed Picture

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode  

Diagnostic ambiguities surrounding Asperger's syndrome are discussed in a historical context; two main subtypes are distinguished according to whether coping mechanisms are predominantly obsessional or schizoid. A case is reported of a girl, later diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome, who originally showed many characteristics of autism, including echolalia. In the later stages of her treatment, she resembled borderline children in her anxious outpouring of florid fantasy. The transition from the first stage to the second was marked by a fantasy of the bodily projection of her mouth into the therapist. Drawings from the beginning of treatment suggested that the schizoid fantasies characteristic of the second stage were already present, although in unelaborated form. The case is discussed in the context of object relations theory and of historical controversies concerning the relationship of autism to childhood psychosis. It is suggested that the intimate psychodynamic knowledge of a child acquired during therapy can make a contribution to diagnostic classification.

S. Montana Katz  

This article contains a way to foster understanding and dialogue between psychoanalytic perspectives. A model of mental functioning is proposed that uses a concept of unconscious metaphoric processes as its core concept. The model yields a neutral and purely psychoanalytic language capable of expressing the basic concepts and tenets of different psychoanalytic perspectives. It is suggested that through the terms of the language, similarities and differences may be clarified between the perspectives. If the proposed model is successful, it might be employed as a technical and pedagogical tool within psychoanalysis, as well as a psychoanalytic base from which to engage in interdisciplinary dialogue.

Metaphor and metonymy are the primary and crucial cognitive tools of unconscious thought. responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Centrality of Empathy in Psychoanalysis

Paul Ornstein M.D.

Paul Ornstein

Paul Ornstein  

This article presents a condensed appraisal of Kohut's groundbreaking conception of the method and the boundaries of psychoanalysis, republished here with permission. Kohut reinstated Freud's original claim that empathy was the only way to enter the inner world of another and he extended and redefined its functions. Empathy not only permits a prolonged, sustained entry into the inner world of the patient, it also designates the boundaries of psychoanalysis as a pure psychology—in the sense that only what is accessible via empathy is psychoanalysis. A description of empathy and its functions are then presented in a more detailed fashion, and include a highly abbreviated clinical example. In this example, a prolonged theory-driven analysis ultimately gave way to a search for the patient's subjective experience and its understanding, leading to a therapeutically more effective analytic approach.

Fantasy Play as the Conduit for Change in the Treatment of a Six-Year-Old Boy With Asperger's Syndrome

Katharine Gould

Katharine Gould

Katharine Gould  

Using a psychoanalytic approach, I demonstrate how I was able to uncover the keen longing for attachment that lay underneath David's unrelated and alienating behaviors—behaviors that repelled his peers and made him an unmanageable puzzle for his parents and teachers. My clinical notes (from a two-and-a-half year treatment of once-a-week sessions), indicate the gradual process of guiding him into play by introducing first dialogue and then characters into his mechanized rituals until he begins to tell his own story. Over time, this experience of reciprocity enabled David to feel safe and empowered in the external world, where formerly he had been a helpless and angry outcast. An unplanned early termination first threatens to interrupt his progress but ultimately provokes an unexpected demonstration by David of what he had learned.

[[RunningHead]]

Psychoanalyzing a Vulcan: The Importance of Mental Organization in Treating Asperger's Patients

Alan Sugarman

Alan Sugarman

Alan Sugarman  

The opinion that psychoanalysis is of little value in treating patients suffering from Asperger's syndrome is a relatively common one, even among fellow psychoanalysts. Several reasons have been suggested to account for this including the discrediting of psychoanalytic treatment for patients in the autistic spectrum because of Bettelheim's (1967) mistaken blaming of the condition on poor parenting or the assumption that a biochemically based disorder cannot benefit from a psychologically oriented treatment. This article suggests that a third reason has to do with the underlying model of mutative action used by many current day psychoanalysts. Implicit in most modern day Freudian work is a model of mutative action that prioritizes verbal interpretation and emphasizes the gaining of insight into unconscious mental content. Viewing the psychoanalytic task as deciphering the unconscious meaning of the patient's verbalizations ignores the problem that Asperger's patients have with mentalizing or developing a theory of mind. This article suggests that psychoanalysts shift their emphasis to promoting a process of insightfulness defined as the equivalent of mentalization as it occurs in the psychoanalytic situation. Insightfulness is similar to the Kleinian emphasis on promoting higher order symbolic thinking. The psychoanalytic treatment of a patient suffering from Asperger's syndrome is described to illustrate how the psychoanalyst works to promote insightfulness and how this approach differs from trying to uncover the hidden, unconscious content presumed to lie at the depths of the psyche. The patient described also illustrates the higher end of the Asperger's spectrum and the need not to let the character defenses that develop to cope with such a debilitating disorder not obscure the essential constitutional basis of the patient's difficulties even though, of course such limitations will become components of compromise formations.

A Voice Lost, A Voice Found: After the Death of the Analyst

Robin Deutsch

Robin Deutsch

Robin Deutsch  

What is the fate of the analytic life created by the analysand and the analyst when only half the dyad remains? This essay explores the author's experience in the wake of her analyst's sudden death. After experiencing the sudden loss of her analyst, the author loses contact with that part of herself that had come to access thoughts and feelings and share them with a particular other. She describes a process of alteration in her relationship with the person, transferential and real, of her analyst, focusing on a series of dreams after her analyst's death that illustrates how retaining and cementing her relationship with her deceased analyst, through internalization, facilitated the return of her analysand voice. The author explores the confounding variable of entering another analytic relationship within the context of a traumatic ending to her previous analysis.

Pregnancy as a Resistance

Mary Otte Ph.D.

Mary Otte

Mary Otte  

The author discuss four patients who were pregnant during their analyses and wanted to abort treatment. Each patient struggled with both conscious and unconscious fantasies of a destructive mother/analyst that could interfere with their well-being with envious retaliation and/or damage to the baby. The origins of these fantasies were unresolved preoedipal and oedipal conflicts and the patients' own destructive wishes. These issues were worked through with various degrees of success, dependent on the persistence of a delusional transference.

Susan Sherkow  

This article describes a psychoanalytically informed dyadic approach to treatment of children with autism spectrum disorder that both engages the child on a psychodynamic level and works toward addressing the impact on the mother and the mother–child relationship resulting from the child's diagnosis and developmental differences. Some Thoughts About the Psychological Issues Related to Assisted Reproductive Technology

Malkah Notman M.D.

Malkah Notman

Malkah Notman  

The use of assisted reproductive technology has increased enormously. The new techniques sometimes make possible babies with unusual genetic combinations and definitions of motherhood, fatherhood, and family. Psychoanalytic literature on the experiences and effects of these is relatively new, although infertility has been the subject of more attention. The issues raised by these techniques and their effects are reviewed in this article. Attitudes continue to change and approaches which seemed strange and possibly problematic have become more accepted in a relatively brief period.

Empathy in Psychoanalytic Theory and Practice

Donald Grant and Edwin Harari

Edwin Harari

Australia

Fitzroy, Australia

Edwin Harari  

With the exception of Self Psychology, empathy has not been a major theoretical concept in psychoanalysis. Freud's (1921) definition of empathy implies it is a necessary condition for an analytic process to develop (p. 110, n. 2). Most psychoanalytic theories have side-stepped this issue by including empathy under various assumed names. We have discussed some of these in the theories of a number of psychoanalysts within the British Psychoanalytical Society. We have illustrated some of these theoretical issues with a clinical example.

Empathy—The Indispensable Ingredient in the Impossible Profession

David Kitron

David Kitron


David Kitron   David Kitron is a supervising clinical psychologist, teaches and supervises at the Tel-Aviv University Program of Psychotherapy, works as scientific editor for Bookworm publishing house, and is in private practice.

Introduction

“Poetry is what gets lost in translation” (Robert Frost)

“Poetry is what is gained in translation” (Joseph Brodsky)

Salman Rushdie (2009), in his article on film adaptations of novels, argues that the question of essence remains at the heart of the adaptive act. He believes that “As individuals, as communities, as nations, we are the constant adapters of ourselves, and must constantly ask ourselves the question…what are the things we cannot ever give up unless we wish to cease to be ourselves?” (p. 11). Rushdie defines adaptation broadly, as a general term that includes translation, migration, and metamorphosis, “all the things by which one thing becomes another” (p. 3). I think we could add psychotherapy to this list. A basic ingredient in Rushdie's recipe for adaptation, very much like psychotherapy, is its being practiced by persons who understand and care for both the old and the new, “who can help the thing adapted to bridge the gulf and shine again in a different light” (p. 2). In therapy, however, the dearest thing is at stake, the essence of one's very selfhood. According to Winnicott (1963), this very essence, the core of one's true self, faces a fatal threat when it ceases to remain incommunicado. When we ask patients to expose their innermost experience to us, empathy becomes the indispensable ingredient that enables the true self to be safeguarded. And if, according to Winnicott (1963), the therapist–patient environment, like the mother–infant environment, is to be facilitative and not impinging, then empathy means surrendering, in Ghent's (1990) terms, but not submitting the therapist's own subjectivity in favor of the patient's subjectivity.

If the patient's inner core is respected, psychotherapy, like translation, is freed of the dictum “translator equals traitor,” and ceases to be a reductive, restrictive endeavor. Then we can adopt (or adapt!) Paul Ricoeur's (2004) notion of linguistic hospitality, an approach that, both in principle and in practice, does not aspire for universality, but accepts the other individual's unique essence. This approach respects the fact that no absolute, perfect translation can ever be attainable. The analogy to empathy and its asymptotic character of getting closer, but never reaching, the absolute, as described by Kohut (1981b), is easy to draw. Like translation, like empathy, all the mediator (therapist/translator) can do is offer his roof and do his best as a benevolent host to the object. Neither translation nor empathic understanding can aspire to be identical to the original (language/subjective mind) but both can do their best to offer themselves as successful adaptations.

Lester Lenoff LCSW

The clinical provision of a “non-interpretive holding environment” described by Joyce Slochower (1991), a Relational psychoanalyst whose work is the subject of this article, has been associated by Stephen Mitchell (1988) with “developmental tilt.” Slochower (1999) notes the description of developmentally tilted frameworks as “models [that] allow the analyst to gratify the patient in the context of addressing early deprivations and tend to play out patient's and analyst's fantasies of a magical cure” (p. 710).

Yet the clinical ambience of Slochower's (1996c) holding stance presents a complex, nonmagical process that “requires that I tolerate a particularly difficult level of strain, self-doubt, and conflict about maintaining an idealized illusion of parental attunement … that renders [the patient] highly reactive to my actual failures” (p. 145), “in order for the patient to acquire a more even sense of relatedness … a complex interplay between holding and failure in holding must take place” (p. 136, emphasis added).

These descriptions mandate a reconsideration of Slochower's use of Winnicott's (1960) concept and its clinical application. This is of interest to self psychologists because Kohut's (1959) concepts of empathy and deficit (A. Ornstein and Ornstein, 2005) have been stereotyped, along with holding, as supporting such a tilt in theory and practice (see Lenoff, 2003). Following a synopsis of Slochower's work, I offer a self psychological viewpoint as a means of adding an expanded or alternative understanding of the clinical process. Although I am writing as a self psychologist, I speak only for myself. Many self psychologists, including those I cite, might take issue with the use I make of Kohut's texts, or their own. With the personal context in mind, what I hope is to provide is a sensibility of theory and practice which readers might try on for size to support or expand their capacity to work with patients.

Given the breadth of Slochower's (2004) writing on holding, as a concept (1991, 1996a), as a metaphor (1996b), and as a clinical stance (1992, 2004), limitations of space dictate that I focus on her treatment of Karen,1 “a hateful borderline patient” (1992, p. 72). “Where Do the Ova Go?” An Analytic Exploration of Fantasies Regarding Infertility

Aisha Abbasi M.D.

Aisha Abbasi

Aisha Abbasi  

It is my intention, in this article, to present an analytic exploration, through clinical material, of a patient's fantasies about her infertility, including what she thought had caused it, what she imagined was happening in her body as she tried to conceive, and how these fantasies about her infertility were seen to be vitally linked to difficulties in her functioning in other areas of her life. Even though the patient conceived with the help of assisted reproductive technology (ART), my focus in this article will not be extensively on the challenges and dilemmas that ART often brings up, but rather more on what we learned about how my patient experienced herself in her struggle with infertility. I also hope to demonstrate that an evolving understanding of these fantasies helped her understand her inhibitions in the areas of sexuality, interpersonal interactions, her professional life, and her overall sense of her own autonomy, creativity, well-being, and assertiveness.

Time to Say Goodbye: On Time, Trauma, and Termination

Dianne Elise

Dianne Elise

Dianne Elise  

This essay addresses the painful circumstance of the analyst's death in the midst of an analysis. Through a series of dreams after her analyst's death, Deutsch (this issue) works hard to recover from the shock of sudden loss, and to recover her shared dialogue with her lost analyst within the context of a new analytic relationship. In contending with death and mortality, one is made acutely aware of the peculiar relationship we each have with temporality—the multifaceted quality of our complex, ambivalent relationship to the exigencies of time. Trouble with time shows itself most especially in our difficulties with the emotional pain of saying goodbye.

Human development is inseparable from our development in relation to time, and our capacity to cope with time is always vulnerable to regression in the face of trauma. For adults troubled by time, analysis offers a space for mourning losses and for moving forward into the rhythm of time. A full termination phase creates an expanse of time—real and psychic—to say goodbye. The analyst's participation is crucial in insuring that this process of parting unfolds to its fullest extent, allowing for mortality to weave its way through the tapestry of termination.

Reconnecting Psychoanalysis to Mainstream Psychology: Metaphor as Glue

Robert Bornstein Ph.D. and Nikaya Becker-Matero M.A.

Nikaya Becker-Matero

Nikaya Becker-Matero  

In recent decades, psychoanalysts have examined the role of metaphor in psychodynamic theory and therapy, but the uses of metaphor in psychoanalytic research have received only modest attention. After briefly reviewing extant psychoanalytic writings on metaphor, we discuss how research from outside psychoanalysis (i.e., studies of embodied affect–space links, mental images and prototypes, and associative networks) can inform us about the nature of metaphor. We then explore the ways that metaphor deepens our understanding of psychodynamic research and its implications, focusing on metaphoric definitions of concepts, and the metaphoric features of experimental manipulations and outcome assessments. Implications of a metaphoric perspective for the empirical testing of psychoanalytic concepts are discussed, and future directions for exploration in this area are described.

Mauricio Cortina   Mauricio Cortina, M.D., is director, Attachment and Human Development Center, Washington School of Psychiatry and a Faculty member at the Institute of Contemporary Psychotherapy and Psychoanalaysis, Washington, DC.

Introduction

Heinz Kohut and John Bowlby, working independently, contributed to a paradigm shift within psychoanalysis. Their combined work dramatically changed the way many psychoanalysts understand the effect of parent–child relationships on human development, as well as the very nature of psychopathology. This, in turn, transformed clinical practice as their ideas spread and many analysts became more emotionally responsive, creating a friendlier, more respectful therapeutic ambiance.

Essential to both men's thinking is a deep and abiding belief in the central need for relationships beginning at birth and lasting throughout life. Further, they recognized how a parent's responsiveness to a child's needs for comfort and protection plays a crucial role in the child's psychological development with an outcome of either healthy adjustment or psychopathology hanging in the balance.

In articulating these positions, they differed with the mainstream psychoanalytic views of their time. The classical psychoanalytic perspective focused on intrapsychic conflict over a set of drives, libido, and aggression. In both the theory and practice of the prevailing Freudian tradition, the greatest attention was given to exploring a patient's instinctual life as expressed in fantasy, rather than to actual experiences during childhood. Kohut and Bowlby came to see that such an intrapsychic focus on drives and fantasies came at the expense of recognizing important developmental needs for relatedness. Also, they saw how an exclusive preoccupation with elucidating a patient's intrapsychic conflicts could interfere with the therapist's ability to grasp the very real and adverse impact of unresponsive (or abusive) parenting during childhood.

Kohut's and Bowlby's individual journeys as psychoanalytic clinicians and revolutionary theorists were dramatically different, yet both men broke with the predominant psychoanalytic dogma of their time and came to essentially the same viewpoint concerning the deep importance of relationships. Their body of work has proven to have tremendous impact on the clinical practice of psychoanalysts and psychodynamic psychotherapists over the last 40 years as they ushered in new ways of interacting with patients that were more compassionate, engaged, and flexible. Metaphor in Psychoanalysis: Bane or Blessing?

Robert Wallerstein M.D.

Robert Wallerstein

Robert Wallerstein  

Since the 1980 book, The Metaphors We Live By, by Lakoff and Johnson, the cognitive–linguistic view of metaphor that they propound has come to be most widely accepted. Its characteristic features are that (a) metaphor is a property of the concept, not the words; (b) its function is to heighten understanding, not simply artistic or aesthetic; (c) it is often not based on similarity; (d) it is ubiquitous in ordinary language, not requiring special talent; and (e) it is an inevitable intrinsic aspect of all human thought and language. This is true of all speech, including the speech in and of psychoanalysis. Metaphor both amplifies and creates meaning. But it can also be misleading and produce conceptual errors of meaning. It should, therefore, not be reified or always taken literally, but should remain flexible and alterable, so that heuristically more relevant and more encompassing metaphor can readily be elaborated.

Introduction

There are many aspects of Kohut's contributions that can be viewed as immensely valuable. His emphasis upon the role of empathy and the selfobject function in childhood development and in the analytic process has more than proved its importance, as attachment studies have revealed the crucial significance of the “dyadic regulation of affect” and many forms of personality disturbance have been shown to be disorders of affect regulation (Mollon, 2001b). Neurobiology has amply validated Kohut's perspective on the relational nurturance of the brain, as well as the mind—showing that the main attachment figure does indeed function as a regulatory part of the child's self-system (Schore, 1994; Mollon, 2001a). Kohut's notion of transmuting internalisation, whereby externally provided psychological functions are gradually internalised to form the structure of the self, his articulation of the line of development of narcissism, with its bifurcation into the poles of mirroring and idealising, its role in the formation of the self-structure of persisting goals and ideals—and his outline of the vertical split in the psyche of narcissistically disordered patients—all these have been outstanding and original contributions with the ability to transform the clinician's practice in myriad benign ways. There is no doubt in my own mind that working in accord with Kohut's empathic perspective, the active use of the imagination to understand the world from the patient's point of view, leads to better results than working otherwise.
